[ALUSI-FULL:v18p30#3/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One explanation is that former flesh and similar parts become dust, while others become bare, decayed bones; dust comes first because its transformation is especially implausible and it derives from visible parts.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p30#3/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, earlier generations were wholly dust, while later generations are bones.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p30#3/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The second أنكم reinforces the first after the long separation from its predicate مخرجون.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p30#3/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The promised outcome is that they will emerge alive from their graves as before, after dying and becoming dust.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p30#3/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفراء والجرمي والمبرد | prefers | They attach إذا to مخرجون; this does not mean emergence occurs at the instant of death, despite Abu Nizar's objection, which al-Sakhawi refutes and al-Suyuti transmits.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p30#3/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh treats the second أنكم as an emphatic بدل of the first; the first predicate is omitted, inferred from the second, and governs إذا. An adverb of time cannot directly predicate of a person unless إخراجكم is understood.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p31/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another parsing makes أنكم مخرجون the subject and إذا متم its predicate, with the clause serving as predicate of the first أن; al-Baḥr calls this easy, and al-Sakhawi attributes it to al-Mubarrad.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p31/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Alusi prefers the parsing reported from al-Farra and his associates as best suited to the Qur'anic word order.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p31/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عبد الله | reports | The reading attributed to ʿAbd Allah omits the first أنكم and reads أيعدكم إذا متم.
[ELMALILI:23:31-41/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | The people dismiss bodily resurrection from dust and bones as impossibly remote, claim worldly life is all there is, and say one generation dies as another is born, so they should enjoy this low life.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p52#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | أيعدكم is an astonished question that shifts their attack from his claim to be a messenger to the message he conveys.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p53/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The promise is that they will be brought out of their graves after death and bodily disintegration, alive with a complete human form for resurrection.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p53/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجرمي والمبرد | reports | Al-Jarmī and al-Mubarrad allow the second أنكم to repeat the first after an intervening clause, adding emphasis to the improbably phrased promise.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p53/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Another possible parsing makes the second أنكم the subject, with the إذا clause as its fronted predicate; that whole clause then predicates the first أنكم.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p53/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The deniers treat death and reduction to dust and bones as states incompatible with life and restoration of the human body, which fuels their incredulity.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p53/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | هيهات explains the preceding promise and is therefore a separate, uncoordinated sentence.
[TABATABAI:23:23-54/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Their question about being brought out after becoming soil and bones refers to resurrection from graves for reckoning and recompense.
[ASAD-NOTES:23:33/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | They dismiss the messenger as an ordinary human and reject his promise that people will be raised after becoming dust and bones.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:31/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Opponents of prophets were often wealthy elites content with the order because it served their interests; they feared afterlife accountability and a society conscious of universal rights and justice would threaten their status.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:31/r7] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Since the Qur’an answers these denials of the prophet’s person and of the afterlife elsewhere, this passage only warns of the rejecters’ painful fate.
[QIRAAT-ER:23:35:4#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · canonical | reports | The segment identifies mittum with kasra on mīm as the standard canonical Form I perfect of the root m-w-t.
[QIRAAT-ER:23:35:4#2/r1] QIRAAT-ER · vw | reports | The canonical variant muttum has ḍamma on mīm, an alternate vocalization of the same root; both forms are accepted.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p123/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | He calls the passage's close with resurrection natural: resurrection is the final link in the sequence of life and its development. | mentions 39:31
[STUDYQURAN:23:35/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The objection that humans reduced to dust and bones can be revived recurs in the cited verses; revival of dead bones is also discussed in two other contexts. | mentions 17:49, 17:98, 23:82, 37:16, 37:53, 56:47, 36:78, 79:11
[STUDYQURAN:23:35/r2] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | “Brought forth” literally means “caused to leave it”: the dead leave the earth where they lie when given life on the Last Day.
[STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r4] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | After recalling worldly blessings, the surah tells of Noah's struggle against his people's denial and rebuke and his journey in the ark.
[STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The opposition of affluent and powerful people to prophets recurs throughout this surah, as elsewhere in the Quran. | mentions 7:59, 7:60, 7:61, 7:62, 7:136

<<end of notes>>

item.text: The main cluster concerns the two occurrences of أنكم: the notes give several syntactic analyses and objections to some of them. I’m keeping those analyses together, with separate questions for the readings, the speakers, and the resurrection claim.
